## 3. Methods

### 3.1. Study area and site selection

The study was conducted across the Naarm/Greater Melbourne region, in sites similar to those sampled in @walsh2009 & @walsh&webb2014. The region has an Oceanic temperate climate exposed to hot dry summers and cool wet winters [@beck2018], and is partially subject to El Nino-Southern Oscilation climate cycles [@nicholls1985; @power1999]. Long-term mean seasonal maximum temperatures range from 25.3 degrees Celsius in summer (January) to 14.2 degrees Celsius in winter (July) [@bom2025]. The region is physiographically diverse with a strong northeast-southwest gradient in precipitation: the west features grassland-dominated basalt plains with *Eucalyptus* open woodlands along stream valleys (mean precipitation \~400-500 mm/year); the east features upland ranges with tall wet sclerophyll *Eucalyptus* forests (mean precipitation up to 1800 mm/year). Land uses within waterway catchments vary from natural, intact, protected water supply catchments to agricultural and forested rural, and urban, leading to waterways that vary from near-pristine to severely degraded. In 2024, the estimated resident population in Greater Melbourne was \~5.3 million [@australianbureauofstatistics2025].

We selected 132 sites for sampling in-stream macroinvertebrates, using a generalised random tessellation stratified balanced matrix [@stevens2004]. Sites were selected to reduce covariance between catchment area (km$^2$), total forest cover (proportion of total forest cover in catchment), total imperviousness (proportion of total impervious cover in catchment), degree of upstream regulation (DoR), and equal representation of Victorian bioregions. The final set of sampling sites covered environmental gradients of total forest cover, total impervious cover, annual mean daily temperature (henceforth referred to as only 'temperature') from the 30 years preceding, and annual mean rainfall runoff (MeanQ) with low multicollinearity between predictors (all pairwise $R^2$ \< 0.5, see `model_data_assembly.qmd` for details). Total forest cover ranged between 0.01 to 99.9%, total impervious cover between 0 and 35.7%, catchment area between 0.7 and 275.9km², temperature between 11.1 and 15.4 °C, and meanQ between 12 to 911 mm/year across all sampled sites [@fig-site_maps; The full list of environmental variables and abbreviations used throughout are listed in Table 1]. Environmental data for each sampled site was retrieved from the Melbourne Water Stream Network Database [@walsh_mwstr2023], which contains the primary data source for total forest cover and total imperviousness.

#### 3.1.1. Attenuated forest and effective impervious cover compilation

The Melbourne water stream network [@walsh_mwstr2023] maps many smaller streams that were unmapped in the stream network data used by earlier studies [@walsh2009; @walsh&webb2014]. Its drainage density across the region is 2.0 km/km2 compared to 0.64 km/km2 for the older data. @walsh_mwstr2023 derived a function for delineating streams of the Melbourne region too small to be sampled for macroinvertebrates (which we hereafter term 'small streams'), as a function of catchment area and mean annual discharge depth. These small streams constitute 67% of the network's stream length. A stream map pruned to exclude these small streams has approximately the same drainage density (0.65 km/km2) as the stream network used by earlier studies. We therefore used the pruned network to calculate alternative weighted measures of forest and impervious cover, in addition to those calculated using the full network, to assess if any differences in inference between this work and earlier work in the same region were attributable to the greater drainage density of the new network data.

The catchments of the stream network were delineated using a 5-m gridcell digital elevation model (DEM, @walsh_mwstr2023), which is used as the basis for estimation of catchment-scale predictors. To weight land-use predictors, the DEM was used to calculate two distance rasters: (1) total flow distance to outlet of the network ($d2ol$), and (2) overland flow distance to the nearest stream ($dL$). For any reach on the stream network with a $d2ol$ of $dWr$ <!--# what is dWr?? -->, the in-stream flow distance of each gridcell in its catchment was calculated as:

$$
dW = d2ol - dL - dWr
$$

For distance weightings involving impervious area (below), @walsh_mwstr2023 delineated urban areas where almost all roofs and roads were connected to a piped stormwater network, and $dL$ of gridcells within these areas was set to the distance of the pipe network outlet to the stream (usually zero), thus assuming no attenuation of impervious effect through sealed drainage systems [@baskhar]. For the pruned network, $dL$ and $dW$ were adjusted to $dLp$ and $dWp$*,* where $dWs$ was the segment of $dW$ flowing along small streams. $dLp$ and $dWp$ approximated the $dL$ and $dW$ estimates of earlier studies [@walsh2009; @walsh&webb2014].

<!--# Why is dLp equal to dL + dWs? Ask Chris about this... -->

$$
dLp = dL + dWs \\
dWp = dW - dWs
$$ {#eq-pruning}

<!--# How was non-independence between vegetation size classes managed? -->

Forest and impervious spatial data were acquired from Nearmap AI data pack (medium & high vegetation \>2 m), covering $25m^2$ resolution gridcells across the Greater Melbourne region. We used forest cover as an environmental predictor to characterise the effect of land clearing from anthropogenic land use (such as agricultural or industrial), implied by measurable forest cover decreases. Specifically, we use an attenuated forest cover measure previously evaluated by @walsh&webb2014 (adapted from @vansickle2008) that weights overland and up-stream flow distances by their exponential decay ([@eq-af_weighting]). $AF$ describes the attenuated forest cover cumulative to a site, which is given by the proportion of total forest within a catchment that has the strongest influence on in-stream macroinvertebrate model predictions, weighting each gridcell ($t$) within a site catchment by the attenuation weighting $A_t$. For both the full and pruned networks, in a catchment of N gridcells, we weighted total forest cover $F_t$ (between $0$ and $25 m^2$) and total gridcell area ($25 m^2$) of each gridcell $t$ [@eq-af_weighting]. We calculated $A_t$ by exponentially weighting the distance (m) of each gridcell $t$ to-stream ($dL_t$) and up-stream ($dW_t$) by half-decay distance (HDD) constants for $L$ (for $dL$, over land) and $W$ (for $dW$, in-stream) [@eq-af_attenuation].

$$
\begin{align}
AF_{(L,W)} &= \frac{\Sigma^N_1 (F_t \cdot A_t)}{\Sigma^N_1 (25 \cdot A_t)}
\end{align}
$$ {#eq-af_weighting}

$$
\begin{align}
A_t &= exp \left(\frac{log(0.5) \cdot dL_t}{L}\right) \cdot exp \left( \frac{log(0.5) \cdot dW_t}{W} \right)
\end{align}
$$ {#eq-af_attenuation}

Due to the computational burden of computing AF variants and fitting models, we identified an initial range of $W$ and $L$ parameters by generating candidate AF data from trial in-stream and overland HDD distances (hereafter referred to as 'parameterisations', and trial combinations thereof referred to as 'variants'). To account for a major windthrow event that caused widespread tree damage [@victoriastategovernment2023], we retrieved 2018 forest cover data for samples taken prior to the 9th of June, 2021, and 2022 forest cover data for samples taken proceeding the event.

We used impervious cover as a measure of sealed surfaces with hydrologically efficient drainage to environmental streams, to characterise the influence of urban runoff associated with increasing impervious surface area [@allan2004; @walsh2005]. We used impervious coverage data classified by @walsh_mwstr2023. EI was calculated using the same weighting approach as for AF, noting that $dL$ for gridcells in urban areas with piped drainage was set to 0 (see above). Because stormwater drains collect water primarily from impervious surfaces, with pervious surfaces generally draining to unpiped subsurface flowpaths, we chose not to use weighted gridcell areas as the denominator, instead dividing the summed, weighted impervious area by total (unweighted) catchment area, consistent with the approach used by @walsh2009. Thus for a catchment of N gridcells, we weighted the impervious area $I_t$ (between 0 and 25m$^2$) in each gridcell $t$, and divided by total catchment area (given by N 25 m$^2$ gridcells) ([@eq-ei_weighting]). For the pruned network, $A_t$ was calculated by eq 2, using $dLp$ and $dWp$ instead of $dL$ and $dW$, respectively. <!--# No dLp or dWp for EI calculations in this study though - should there be?? This means another round of SPARTAN models... --> For calculating EI using the full network, we added a separate attenuation term for $dWs$ ([@eq-ei_attenuation]), as small ephemeral streams dominated by hyporheic flow are likely to have a greater attenuation effect than larger streams \<reference?\> .

<!--# as a combination of building footprint, asphalt, and concrete slab layers derived from Nearmap AI-Pack data for 2022. A relatively small region that was not covered by 2022 data was sourced from various other sources, including the Nearmap 2018 AI-Pack (www.nearmap.com), 2022 Open Street Map (www.openstreetmap.org) road lines, and Google satellite (earth.google.com) imagery [@walsh_mwstr2023]. Imperviousness within each catchment was then estimated from polygons rasterized to 5-m gridcells, subdivided to 1-m gridcells, then measuring total imperviousness as the number of subdivided 1-m gridcells with an impervious surface within each 5-m gridcell, then divided by the total number of gridcell subdivisions (25 per gridcell). -->

<!--# EI was calculated by weighting the importance of impervious surfaces by their overland to-stream ($dL$) and up-stream ($dW$) flow distances from the most down-slope edge of a connected impervious surface network. The attenuated effect of impervious cover ($I_t$) within all up-slope gridcells ($t$) were weighted against the total catchment area ($CA$). We conditionally weighted gridcells containing drainage outlets with a weighting of 1 to account for sealed surfaces that drained directly to-stream, applying the full effect of impervious cover within such gridcells [@walsh2022]. We evaluated the upstream influence of small streams ($sW$) by weighting flow along these streams separately to that of the pruned network ($W$). For the pruned network, $dLp$ and $dWp$ were used instead of $dL$ and $dW$, respectively.  -->

$$
EI_{(L,sW,W)} = \frac{\Sigma^N_1 (I_t \cdot A_t )}{25 \cdot N}
$$ {#eq-ei_weighting}

$$
A_t = exp \left(\frac{log(0.5) \cdot dL_t}{L}\right) \cdot exp \left( \frac{log(0.5) \cdot dsW_t}{sW}\right) \cdot exp \left( \frac{log(0.5) \cdot dW_t}{W} \right)
$$ {#eq-ei_attenuation}

To determine the ideal predictor set for optimising EI and AF, we constructed a list of candidate predictor sets of different environmental covariate combinations. Each candidate predictor set contained a subset of covariates in every predictor set: presence of riffles (H), EI, AF, and meanQ. EI and AF were included as two environmental predictors associated with anthropogenic land use change, capturing most (if not all) of the catchment-level variability in macroinvertebrate distributions attributable to human land use activity [@pusey2003; @allan2004; @walsh2005]. MeanQ was included as a measure of the rainfall each stream catchment would receive and deliver in the absence of human influence, and thus represents the natural hydrology of a stream [@poff1997]. The presence of riffles (0 or 1) was included as a mandatory predictor as the composition of macroinvertebrate assemblages may be greatly influenced by (but not necessarily dependent on) differences between riffle and pool habitats [e.g., @roy2003; @heino2013; @lancaster2010; @walsh2023].

### 3.2. Macroinvertebrate data

#### 3.2.1. Collection and identification

In-stream macroinvertebrates were collected and identified from 132 sites across the Naarm/Melbourne region, by researchers from the University of Melbourne and consultants from GHD in two seasons (Autumn and Spring) of 2021. Sampling was cunducted using EPA Rapid Biodiversity Assessment (RBA) guidelines [@epavictoria2021]. Two 10 meter benthic sweeps were collected from each site, using a $250 \mu m$ mesh sweep net, targeting one edge and riffle environment, or two edges if no riffle could be sampled at a site. All samples were preserved in 100% ethanol and subsampled under dissecting microscope for 10% of the total sample volume to separate macroinvertebrates from benthic debris. If fewer than 300 animals were found in a subsample, additional 10%-of-whole subsamples were taken until 300 animals were counted [@walsh1997]. Any large animals that could be observed in a sample without a dissecting microscope were picked without subsampling (termed a coarse-pick). The final subsample proportion was recorded for each sample and taxon for modelling subsample bias, recording any coarse-picked taxa with a subsample proportion of 1.

To ensure consistency with previous model optimisation datasets with macroinvertebrates in the same region [e.g., @walsh2009; @walsh&webb2014], macroinvertebrates were identified to the taxonomic level in EPA RBA guidelines [@epavictoria2021]. The RBA protocols typically target family-level taxonomy, with exceptions for groups such as Oligochaeta and Acarina (which were identified to higher levels). Specimens of the Chironomidae family were identified further to subfamily (Orthocladiinae, Chironominae and Tanypodinae). Some immature or damaged specimens of groups mostly identified to family were identified at higher levels. These were typically dipteran and trichopteran larvae or pupae, for which distinguishing features were not available. To provide comparability with previous studies, we calculated SIGNAL score from each sample using a modified biotic index with refinements to the Victoria region, in accordance with the State Environment Protection Policy for Waters of Victoria (SEPP WoV) [@epavictoria2004].

#### 3.2.2. Selecting taxa for optimisation models

To account for species-level variability that could potentially add statistical noise to the family-level response in multi-taxon models [@bailey2001; @lenat2001; @jones2008], we selected a subset of families from the total dataset that were likely to have consistent response patterns between family-level and species-level in a separate dataset \[Wilkins et al., unpublished data\]. We inferred responses by extracting posterior regression coefficient estimates ($\beta$) for previously-optimised EI and AF from fitted multi-taxon models, with both family- and species-level taxonomic resolution. For each family or species' EI and AF $\beta$-estimate, if the posterior 95% Bayesian credible interval did not include 0, then we inferred a positive ($\beta > 0$) or negative ($\beta < 0$) response for that family or species. If the posterior interval did include 0, then we inferred a neutral response ($\beta \approx 0$). Species-level responses were considered consistent with their family-level responses if all species within that family responded similarly to both EI and AF (and presumably more likely to predict well at the family-level). We secondarily excluded families occurring in fewer than 10 sites to remove taxa with very low prevalences [@sor2017; @jiménez-valverde2009]. The final selection of taxa used in analuysis included 45 families, and their specific rationale for inclusion/exclusion is detailed in `taxon_exclusion.qmd`.

### 3.3. Data Analysis

#### 3.3.1. Modeling approach

We inferred model plausibility using Bayesian multi-model inference [@burnham2004] to evaluate hierarchical linear models for the joint occurrence of macroinvertebrate taxa or SIGNAL score, in samples collected across Naarm/Greater Melbourne. Hierarchical modelling within a Bayesian framework improves modelling of macroinvertebrate occurrence patterns by creating a posterior estimate from each taxon's intraspecific patterns, weighted against co-occurrences with other taxa, to reduce uncertainty for taxa that are sparsely observed [@ovaskainen2011; @pollock2014; @wilkinson2019]. To account for unmeasured variables present at each site and time, we assume that the taxon-specific model parameters are random effects linked by regularised assemblage-level hyper-parameters [@gelman2006; @gwinn2018], thereby fitting model coefficients by pulling estimates for all taxa closer to the assemblage-level mean [@mcelreath2020statistical].

Posterior model estimates were fitted using the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) of Stan [@gelman2015; @carpenter2017; @standevelopmentteam2022]. Multi-taxon models were derived from 4000 Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) iterations, discarding the first 2000 as burn-in, and SIGNAL models were run for 2000 iterations, discarding the first 1000. All models were run using 4 chains with parallel processing. We assessed the stability and efficiency of each model by inspecting diagnostic outputs relating to convergence and posterior sampling efficiency. To achieve convergence conditions recommended by @vehtari2021, parameters were tuned such that there was no incidence of divergent transitions, all parameter $\hat{R}$ values less than 1.01 (with convergence implied at $\hat{R} = 1$), all parameter bulk and tail effective sample sizes (ESS) greater than 400, and the Effective Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information (EBFMI) is greater than 0.3.

The NUTS sampler control option for adapt_delta was adjusted to 0.9 to allow greater exploration of posterior distributions with highly-constrained parameter spaces (such as covariance matrices, see @mcelreath2020statistical) and eliminate divergent transitions. We also avoided thinning the posterior distribution as a means of controlling autocorrelation between chains [@link2012]. Models were run on the SPARTAN high-performance cloud computing infrastructure (Intel(R) Xeon(R) GOLD 6448H processor \@ 2.40 GHz [@lafayette2016spartan]), with 300GB RAM and 12 hours walltime allocated per model.

#### 3.3.2. Statistical models for taxon occurrences and SIGNAL score

The multi-taxon model was specified as a hierarchical multi-level model with a Bernoulli probability distribution function for predicting the occurrences (presence = 1, absence = 0) of each taxon $j$ in each sample $i$. We fitted observations to a logit-transformed linear function, given by $\mu_{i,j}$, and composed of random effects relating to the sampling protocols, fixed effects fitted to environmental covariates, a residual spatial effect, and an uncorrelated residual error term [@eq-multi-taxon_lp]. We specified transformed covariates or environmental predictors where transformation improved the evenness of data point across all other gradients. EI was included as a covariate $I$ ($log[EI_i + 0.1^{4}]$, scaled), while meanQ and catchment area (CA) were log-transformed and represented as $Q$ ($log[MeanQ_i]$, scaled) and $C$ ($log[CA_i]$, scaled). AF, temperature and DoR were included as non-transformed covariates $F$ ($AF$, scaled), $T$ (temperature, scaled) and $D$ ($DoR$, scaled), respectively. To cater for taxa with responses to various intermediate levels of discharge [@carvallo2022], we included the quadratic effect of meanQ as $Q²$. The arrangement of each predictor set was denoted by $\gamma$ in [@eq-multi-taxon_lp].

The likelihood of occurrence for each taxon was defined as an N-mixture model, adapting the approach from @royle2004 (eq. 2) to account for sampling bias arising from unequal subsampling effort between samples (as well as between taxa that were picked from the whole sample, henceforth called 'coarsepicks'). This implementation permits modelling likelihood ($p_{i,j}$) as the unobserved probability of occurrence in the environment ($P(Y_{i,j}|\mu_{i,j})$), implied by the observed occurrence of each taxon within samples ($y_{i,j}$) given a particular sub-sample proportion ($\pi_{i,j}$). Assuming that the odds of encountering taxon $j$ from sample $i$ is directly proportional to $\Pi_{i,j}$, then the total probability of occurrence is given by $P(y_{i,j}) = P(Y_{i,j} | \pi_{i,j})$, which is expressed as a log-odds function with $logit(P(y_{i,j}| \pi_{i,j})) = \mu_{i,j} + log(\pi_{i,j})$.

The model contains three random effects (denoted by $\alpha$) accounting for differences arising from taxon identity ($\alpha^{(taxon)}$) for each taxon $j$ with a global hyperparameter. Within-site level effects ($\alpha^{(site)}$) were modeled for each site $k$ encompassing sample $i$ with taxon $j$, with site-level hyperparameters governing the parameter location. Seasonal effects ($\alpha^{(season)}$) were modelled for each season $s$ relating to sample $i$ and taxon $j$, governed by a season-specific location hyperparameter. The JSDM structure was implemented as a correlated-slopes model, leveraging the co-occurrence of taxa to improve regression slope estimates [@ovaskainen2011]. All fixed-effects $\beta$ parameter estimates were specified using an assemblage-level multivariate normal hyper-distribution, where $\beta_m$ is the mean estimate for the $m^{th}$ $\beta$ parameter vector (i.e., environmental variable) across all observations for predictor set $\gamma$ (See \<\>appendix\<\> for full details of candidate model sets). Uncorrelated error ($\epsilon$) was specified with a non-hierarchical prior for each taxon $j$ within each sample $i$.

We accounted for spatial dependence by specifying a Multivariate Conditional Autoregressive (MCAR) model, adapted from Equation 4 in @gelfand2003 (originally described in @mardia1988). This specification permits smooth estimation for the weighting of residual spatial autocorrelation (rSAC) as a function of two parameters: (1) the overland exponential decay rate (given by $\lambda$), and (2) the residual effect of neighbouring sites as a multivariate random-walk model [@codling2008, @crase2012], given by $\Delta$. We first determined the scaled Haversine distance between sites from latitude and longitude coordinates to compute the symmetric proximity matrix $M_{[k,k]}$, which was inversely and exponentially weighted by the global parameter $\lambda$ to create a weighted proximity matrix prior $W_{[k,k]}$. The mean site-level rSAC was modeled by the parameter $\mu_\Delta$ for each site $k$, fitted across each neighbourhood row vector $k'$ (not including the diagonal site identity, $k = k'$). The overall taxon- and site-specific rSAC effect ($\Delta_{k,j}$) was derived from a non-centered hierarchical prior with location determined by the taxon-specific rSAC effect $\Delta^{(taxon)}_j$.

$$
\begin{align}
y_{i,j} &\sim Bernoulli(p_{i,j}) \\
logit(p_{i,j}) &= \mu_{i,j} + log(\pi_{i,j})\\
\mu_{i,j} &= \alpha^{(taxon)}_j + \alpha^{(site)}_{k[i],j} + \alpha^{(season)}_{s[i],j} + \sum_{m=1}^\gamma \beta_{m,j}X_{m,k} +  \Delta_{k[i],j} + \epsilon_{i,j}
\end{align}
$$ {#eq-multi-taxon_lp}

For SIGNAL score models, we specified likelihood as a hierarchical single-level model with a Gaussian probability distribution function to estimate the sample-level SIGNAL score with an expected range of 2 to 8 [@chessman1995]. Uncorrelated error ($\sigma$) was specified as a global variance estimator (rather than $\epsilon$ in the multi-taxon model). Because calculation of the SIGNAL score index incorporates relative abundances as a graded score, subsample error correction was not implemented in the model structure, and fixed effects slopes were drawn from a univariate normal prior for each sample-specific SIGNAL score $i$ ([@eq-signal_lp]).

$$
\begin{align}
y_{i} &\sim Normal(\mu_{i}, \sigma) \\
\mu_{i} &= \alpha^{(global)} + \alpha^{(site)}_{k} + \alpha^{(season)}_{s} + \sum_{m=1}^\gamma \beta_{m}X_{m,k} +  \Delta_{k}
\end{align}
$$ {#eq-signal_lp}

Parameters were specified using weakly-informative priors to improve sampling efficiency. For most normally-distributed priors, we selected an expected mean and standard deviation that allowed the NUTS sampler to "explore" the posterior distribution of each parameter. Unless otherwise specified, all normally-distributed priors were initialized as a standard normal prior (i.e., $Normal(0, 1)$, then adjusted to meet convergence and efficiency requirements [@standevelopmentteam2022], and posterior distributions were sufficiently explored by the MCMC sampler. To improve exploration of posterior distributions with multidimensional parameter spaces, we specified non-centered parameterisations that separated the location and scale of parameter estimates. This was achieved by modelling a latent location parameter transformed by a mixture of pooled and unpooled hyperpriors or an adaptive prior [@standevelopmentteam2022, @mcelreath2020statistical] (See `model_optimisation.qmd` for a detailed rationale for each selected prior).

#### 3.3.3. AF and EI optimisation

The most plausible model predictor set was determined by Bayesian multi-model selection, reporting the Effective Log-Point Predictive Density (ELPD) as an estimate of model plausibility. ELPD estimates the out-of-sample predictive accuracy by aggregating posterior log-likelihoods for each data point, balancing model fit and complexity similarly to Akiake Information Criterion [@vehtari2017]. To approximate ELPD for each model, we performed Leave-One-Out Cross Validation (LOO-CV) using the `loo` library [@vehtari2024], reporting the ELPD bootstrap differences (δELPD) and normal-approximated difference standard error (δSE) as a measure of model plausibility. An δELPD value equal to 0 implies the model is comparatively the most plausible of the models evaluated [@vehtari2017]. Models with δELPD greater than 4 were considered similar if the normal approximation of ELPD differences (δELPD/δSE) was greater than 2, indicating the ELPD 95% CI for that model encompassed 0 (and was therefore equally plausible to the best-performing model). Due to underestimation of LOO-approximated δSE when δELPD is small [@sivula], any model with δELPD \< 4 was considered equally most-plausible.

We inferred optimal attenuation distances by approximating the expected data-generating AF and EI parameterisations (i.e., the M-open setting, as the optimal parameterisation variant is not necessarily one of the candidate variants) from fitted Bayesian models. We first approximated ELPD via LOO-CV to determine the range of plausible AF and EI variants, then determined the optimal predictor weights for AF ($L$ and $W$) and EI ($W$, $sW$ and $L$) by comparing model weights from Pseudo-Bayesian Model Averaging with Bayesian bootstrapping (P-BMA+) [@hoge2020; @vehtari2024]. The model weights were drawn from 1000 bootstrap samples with a uniform probability shape ($\alpha = 1$). Models with the greatest weights are expected to best represent the true data-generating process, with weights close to 1 implying that a model is most true [@yao2018]. Finally, we calculated the weighted mean HDD for each trial ($x$), weighted by each P-BMA+ model averaging weight ($w$) from each fitted model $i$, to approximate the expected true data-generating HDD distance ($\bar{X}(\bar{w})$) for $n$ weights (i.e., AF: $L$ and $W$; EI: $W$, $sW$ and $L$) ([@eq-weighted_mean]).

$$
\bar X_{(\bar w)} = \sum_{i = 1}^n (x_{i} * w_i)
$$ {#eq-weighted_mean}

#### 3.3.4. Modelled data visualisation and inference

To identify the influence of mapping extent and biological endpoint, we inferred optimal weightings for EI and AF in two steps: (1) identifying best-performing variants within multi-taxon and SIGNAL with broad-range variant trials, and (2), approximating the true data-generating HDD distance from P-BMA+ weights [@hoge2020; @vehtari2024], using an exhaustive range of HDD variants. For AF, we specified an initial broad-range trial variant array with combinations of (in meters) $L \in \{0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\}$ and $W \in \{200, 400, 800, 1600\}$, which we visualised as contour graphs for the matrix $[L \cdot W]$ and z-axis from model δELPD/δSE values. The true data-generating HDD distances were determined from the P-BMA+ weighted-average of $L$ and $W$, from an exhaustive variant matrix with trial HDDs of $L \in \{0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 48, 64\}$ and $W \in \{200, 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400, 1600\}$.

The previously optimised EI metric by @walsh2009 found that weighting by $W$ did not improve their model predictive performance. We therefore included models with unweighted $W$ and $sW$, denoted by $\infty$ (or Inf), to review weighting by in-stream HDD in the multi-taxon model context. For the 3-dimensional variant array of trial EI $[W \cdot sW \cdot L]$, we visualised the best-performing model variants using P-BMA+ aggregated across each $W$, $sW$ and $L$ respectively. We specified initial broad-range trial variant arrays with combinations of (in meters) $W \in \{4800, 6400, 12800, 25600, \infty \}$, $sW \in \{16, 64, 200, 800, 3200, \infty\}$, and $L \in \{1, 4, 16, 64\}$. The true data-generating HDD distances were determined from the P-BMA+ weighted-average of $L$ and $sW$, from an exhaustive matrix with trial parameterisations of $L \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 48, 64, 128\}$ and $sW \in \{2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200\}$.
